Operator: Good day, and welcome to the NexWave Communications Q3 2023 Earnings Conference Call. All participants are currently in a listen-only mode. After the speakers' presentation, there will be a question-and-answer session. To ask a question during the session, please press star then one on your telephone keypad. To withdraw your question, press star then two. As a reminder, this conference is being recorded.

I would now like to turn the call over to Sarah Thompson, Head of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

Sarah Thompson: Thank you, Operator. Good morning, everyone, and welcome to NexWave Communications' Q3 2023 Earnings Conference Call. Joining me on the call today are Alex Rivera, Chief Executive Officer; Jordan Lee, Chief Financial Officer; Taylor Kim, Chief Network Officer; Morgan Patel, Chief Commercial Officer; and other members of our leadership team.

Before we begin, I would like to remind you that today's discussion may contain forward-looking statements. These statements are based on management's current expectations and are subject to risks and uncertainties that could cause actual results to differ materially. Please refer to our SEC filings for a more complete discussion of these risks.

Alex Rivera: Thank you, Sarah, and good morning, everyone. I am excited to share our Q3 results, which reflect our commitment to innovation and customer satisfaction. We achieved strong performance across several key areas. First, our revenue growth exceeded expectations with a diversified mix highlighting resilience in wireless and media. Second, we continue to see strong adoption of our new 5G fixed wireless access and streaming bundles, leading to significant subscriber gains and revenue uplift. Third, our focus on subscriber acquisition efficiencies has yielded impressive cost reductions. Fourth, we are making significant strides in 5G network deployment and spectrum optimization. Fifth, our efforts in content and media are paying off with robust profitability and subscriber momentum. Sixth, we are strategically investing in enterprise services and emerging technologies like IoT and edge computing, and finally, we are exploring advanced spectrum allocation to fuel future growth.

Jordan Lee: Thank you, Alex. Now, let's move on to the financial results. Our revenue for the quarter reached $28.5 billion, an increase of 4.2% compared to the same period last year and 2.1% quarter-over-quarter. Adjusted EBITDA was $12.1 billion, resulting in a margin of 42.3%, up 120 basis points year-over-year. We are diligently managing our costs and optimizing our capital allocation. Capital expenditures amounted to $4.5 billion this quarter, primarily allocated to 5G infrastructure, fiber deployment, and content acquisition.

Good morning, everyone, and thank you for joining our Q3 2023 earnings call for NexWave Communications. Before diving deeper, let's break down our revenue mix by segment. This analysis underscores the resilience and diversification of our portfolio across wireless, broadband, media and entertainment, and enterprise services, as we continue to execute on our "Connect & Create" strategy amid a dynamic telecom and media landscape.

Our revenue mix remains heavily weighted toward high-margin consumer services, but we're seeing accelerating contributions from growth vectors like 5G standalone deployments, fixed wireless access, and direct-to-consumer streaming. Wireless mobile made up 42% of total revenue at $11.97 billion, up 5.8% year-over-year and 1.9% quarter-over-quarter, with a two-point mix shift. This remains our largest segment, driven by postpaid mobility, which accounted for 72% of wireless revenue. Postpaid ARPU rose 3.1% year-over-year to $58.40, fueled by premium 5G plans bundled with unlimited high-speed data and our new UltraWave mmWave offerings in urban markets. We added 1.2 million postpaid phone net adds—our best Q3 in three years—thanks to aggressive device promotions around the iPhone 15 series and Samsung Galaxy S24 pre-orders. Prepaid grew modestly at 1.8%, with ARPU stable at $42.20, supported by our MVNO partnerships similar to those with Straight Talk.

Key trends include 5G subscribers now representing 68% of our mobile base, up from 55% year-over-year, with standalone core network slicing enabling low-latency services like cloud gaming via our Xbox integration. Legacy 3G and 4G voice revenues declined 12% year-over-year as we sunset spectrum. Regionally, U.S. operations, which are 85% of the segment, grew 6.5% on 5G FWA pilots in rural markets, competing head-on with T-Mobile's offerings. In Europe, via our Vodafone JV, revenues were flat due to regulatory pricing pressures in Germany, but Latin America, at 10% mix, surged 15% on 5G auctions in Brazil. Strategically, we're investing $2.8 billion in Open RAN this year to cut capex by 15% long-term, positioning us like Verizon's vendor diversification push.

Broadband and wireline came in at 28% of total revenue, $7.98 billion, up 6.4% year-over-year and 2.7% quarter-over-quarter, with a one-point mix shift. This was a standout performer, with fiber-to-the-home now 45% of our 32 million broadband subs, up from 38% year-over-year. Average revenue per user climbed 4.2% to $72.50, driven by 1-2 Gbps speed tiers and bundling with our NexStream video service. We passed 2.5 million new homes with XGS-PON fiber in Q3, targeting 55% FTTH penetration by 2025—mirroring Comcast's DOCSIS 4.0 ramp but with pure fiber economics. FWA contributed $450 million, or 6% of the segment, growing 25% year-over-year as a complement to fiber in underserved areas, much like AT&T's AirFiber success. Churn remained elite at 0.9%, below industry averages. Regionally, North America drove 78% of growth, while our APAC fiber joint ventures in India with Reliance Jio added 300k subs amid surging demand for hybrid work. Initiatives include AI-driven network optimization via our Nexus AI platform, reducing opex by 8%, and edge caching for lower latency—critical for competing in a world of Zoom and Microsoft Teams dominance.

Media and entertainment represented 18% of total revenue at $5.13 billion, up 8.2% year-over-year and 3.5% quarter-over-quarter, gaining two mix points. This was our fastest-growing segment, reflecting the convergence of telecom and media. DTC streaming via NexStream SVOD hit 28 million paid subs, up 12% year-over-year, with ARPU at $14.80 thanks to ad-supported tiers, which are 35% of the base, and bundles with mobile plans—similar to Warner Bros. Discovery's Max strategy. Content licensing and linear TV added $1.2 billion, bolstered by our Paramount+ carriage deal and original IP like the WaveFront series. Advertising revenues jumped 22% to $850 million, powered by connected TV ad tech and our DSP integrations with The Trade Desk. Trends show SVOD churn at 4.2%, an industry low, driven by personalization algorithms using telecom data insights. Regionally, U.S. at 60% and Europe at 25% led, but we're scaling in APAC with localized content for Indonesia and Australia markets. Strategically, $1.5 billion in content capex targets 40 million subs by 2025, leveraging 5G multicast for live sports efficiency.

Enterprise services were 10% of total revenue at $2.85 billion, up 2.1% year-over-year and 0.8% quarter-over-quarter, with a one-point mix decline. This showed stable growth, with $1.1 billion from 5G private networks and SD-WAN for Fortune 500 clients like manufacturing firms adopting Industry 4.0. Cloud interconnect revenues, partnering with AWS Direct Connect, grew 10%, but legacy PBX declined 5%. Our IoT platform connected 15 million devices, up 18% year-over-year. Regionally, enterprise is U.S.-heavy at 70%, but EMEA growth via Deutsche Telekom synergies is promising. We're prioritizing hyperscaler adjacencies and edge computing to boost margins to 45% EBITDA.

Other revenues, including advertising and nascent IoT, were 2% at $0.57 billion, up 1.5% year-over-year but down slightly quarter-over-quarter.

This mix shift—with wireless and media gaining four points combined at legacy's expense—highlights our pivot to high-ARPU, data-centric revenues. We're on track for $115-118 billion full-year revenue, with 5G and streaming as $10 billion incremental opportunities by 2026. Risks include spectrum costs post-C-Band auctions and cord-cutting pressures, but our $18 billion capex plan—40% on fiber and 5G—de-risks this. Comparable to peers, our wireless growth outpaces T-Mobile's while media scales faster than Disney's Hulu.

Turning now to subscriber acquisition cost trends, or SAC, in dollar terms, which continue to reflect the disciplined execution of our multi-year efficiency program amid a competitive telecom and media landscape. SAC encompasses all direct and indirect costs to onboard a new postpaid mobile, fixed broadband, or converged media subscriber—including marketing spend, device subsidies, sales commissions, retail partnerships, and promotional credits. Excluding one-time enterprise deals, our blended SAC came in at $428 per subscriber in Q3, down 7% quarter-over-quarter from $461 and 12% year-over-year from $486. This marks the sixth consecutive quarter of sequential improvement, bringing our trailing 12-month average to $445—our lowest since the 4G-LTE ramp in 2015.

In wireless, SAC was $412, down 9% year-over-year. Mobile remains our largest acquisition driver, with 1.2 million postpaid net adds in the quarter. SAC here declined from $452 a year ago, driven by a 22% reduction in per-sub device subsidies—now at just $180 on average, thanks to our Bring Your Own Device push, which hit 58% penetration, up from 45% last year. We're subsidizing fewer flagships like the latest iPhone 15 or Galaxy S24 series, focusing instead on mid-tier Androids and our private-label 5G handsets co-developed with Qualcomm. Commission efficiencies shaved another 15% off sales costs, as we shifted 65% of acquisitions to digital channels—our app-based onboarding and targeted Facebook and Instagram ads, powered by our proprietary AI-driven customer propensity models. These models, leveraging first-party data from our 120 million U.S. subs, have boosted conversion rates by 18% while cutting cost-per-click by 24%. Competitively, this positions us well against Verizon's Visible MVNO pricing wars and T-Mobile's aggressive Go5G promos, where their reported SACs remain sticky around $480 due to heavier discounting.

Broadband and converged SAC was $465, down 5% year-over-year. Fixed-line broadband and FTTH net adds totaled 850,000, with SAC improved from $490 YoY but up slightly quarter-over-quarter due to seasonal back-to-school bundling. Key here is our XGS-PON fiber rollout, now covering 35 million homes passed, which allows us to acquire at lower subsidies—$250 average modem waiver versus $320 last year. We're countering cable peers like Comcast's Xfinity Internet price hikes by offering 1 Gbps plans at $70 a month bundled with mobile, driving a 14% ARPU uplift to $128. In converged media bundles—think our TeleStream One package with ad-supported Peacock and Max content—SAC fell 11% to $510, as partnerships with NBCUniversal and Warner Bros. Discovery reduced content acquisition upfronts by 20%. This is critical in a cord-cutting market where U.S. pay-TV subs dropped another 1.5 million industry-wide per Nielsen data.

Geographically, U.S. SAC averaged $435, flat year-over-year but with 8% quarter-over-quarter improvement from optimized holiday pre-spend. Europe, via our Vodafone JV stake, saw SAC dip to 380 euros, or $415 equivalent, down 15% year-over-year, fueled by EU 5G spectrum auctions lowering capex pass-throughs and our migration of 2 million prepaid subs to postpaid via eSIM auto-provisioning. APAC, our growth engine with 3 million net adds in India and Indonesia, held SAC at $320—remarkably efficient due to low device subventions at $120 average and Jio-like digital UPI payment integrations, though rising ad inflation from TikTok competitors nudged it up 3% quarter-over-quarter. LATAM remains challenged at $510, up 4% year-over-year from Claro merger synergies still bedding in, but our Starlink hybrid fixed-wireless offers are starting to inflect, targeting rural Brazil and Mexico with SAC under $400.

Several levers pulled this quarter: digital marketing shift, with 72% of acquisitions now digital, up from 55% year-over-year, with ROI at 4.2 times versus 2.8 times for traditional TV and rooftop. Our Customer Data Platform integrates anonymized telco signals with media viewing habits, enabling hyper-targeted campaigns—like retargeting cord-cutters who've streamed 10 or more hours of NFL on Prime Video. AI and automation deployed GenAI chatbots for 40% of sales funnels, reducing live agent touchpoints by 30% and commissions by $25 per sub. Predictive analytics cut promo leakage—e.g., limiting 24-month contracts to high-LTV segments. Partner ecosystem expanded Affinity programs with Amazon and Best Buy, driving 250,000 adds at 15% below internal SAC. In media, our FAST channels on Roku and Fire TV acquire freemium users at just $15 SAC, with 25% upgrade to paid. Lower SAC pairs with sub-1% monthly postpaid churn, best in class, extending payback periods to 10 months from 14, boosting LTV over CAC ratio to 3.8 times.

These SAC trends underscore our Efficient Growth 2.0 strategy: prioritizing high-ARPU postpaid over volume prepaid, while media bundles combat OTT pure-plays like Netflix, whose CAC reportedly exceeds $100 globally. We're not chasing T-Mobile's sub-3% churn via endless giveaways; instead, 5G-Advanced standalone core and edge computing investments will enable premium services like AR/VR streaming, justifying 5-7% ARPU growth. Looking ahead, we guide Q4 blended SAC to $420-$430, implying another 2-5% sequential decline, barring macro ad slowdowns. Full-year 2024 target remains $430 average, supporting 300 basis points EBITDA margin expansion. This efficiency funds our $18 billion capex plan—heavy on Open RAN trials with Nokia and fiber densification—without compromising 2.5 million total net adds guidance.

Today, I'd also like to dive deep into one of our key growth drivers: the impact of our new product and service launches on revenue and subscriber growth. NexWave is at the forefront of converging telecommunications and media, leveraging our nationwide 5G Standalone network, C-band spectrum holdings, and an expanding content ecosystem to capture share in a market where cord-cutting accelerated to 6.5 million U.S. pay-TV losses year-over-year—per recent Nielsen data—and 5G adoption is surging past 25% penetration globally.

In Q3 alone, our strategic launches generated $1.2 billion in incremental revenue, up 45% quarter-over-quarter and representing 18% of our total service revenue of $6.7 billion. This was fueled by net subscriber adds of 2.8 million, a 32% year-over-year increase, bringing our postpaid mobile base to 112 million and broadband households to 28 million.

First, our 5G Home Fixed Wireless Access product, rolled out in 1,200 new mid-band markets using our 3.45-3.55 GHz C-band spectrum. This addresses underserved rural and suburban segments where fiber deployment lags—think competitors like Comcast's Xfinity but with wireless economics. We added 1.1 million FWA subscribers in Q3, 60% above our internal targets, at an ARPU of $65 a month—10% higher than traditional cable broadband due to unlimited data and 1 Gbps speeds. This drove $285 million in new revenue, with 85% gross margin thanks to our virtualized RAN and Open RAN architecture, which cut capex per sub by 25% versus legacy deployments. Churn here is sub-1%, versus industry 2.5% for FWA, as we're bundling it with our media services. Regionally, U.S. performance was stellar—950k adds in the Midwest and Southeast, where we're outpacing T-Mobile's 5G Home ramp by 20% market share. In Europe, via our joint venture with Vodafone in Germany and the UK, we hit 150k adds, capitalizing on Ofcom's spectrum auctions.

Second, NexWave Stream+, our ad-supported streaming bundle launched in June, integrating our linear TV with FAST channels, Netflix Basic, and Disney+ Hotstar at $25 a month—undercutting Hulu + Live TV by 30%. This taps the $150 billion global SVOD market, projected to grow 12% CAGR through 2027 per PwC. We onboarded 1.2 million streaming subs, with 70% upsell from our mobile base, boosting blended ARPU by $8 to $112 postpaid. Revenue contribution: $420 million, including $120 million from AVOD at a 40% margin, driven by our AI-powered dynamic ad insertion tech. U.S. cord-cutters drove 900k adds, with penetration highest among millennials at 15% attach rate. In APAC, our India rollout via Jio partnerships added 200k, riding the JioTV wave amid 500 million-plus smartphone users. Latin America saw 100k in Brazil and Mexico, where we're partnering with Claro for 5G convergence.

Third, enterprise 5G Private Networks and Edge services, targeting the Industrial IoT boom—think manufacturing and logistics, akin to Verizon's 5G Edge but with our media overlay for AR/VR training apps. We secured 450 enterprise contracts, adding 500k IoT/M2M connections and $495 million in B2B revenue, with 75% recurring from managed services. Average deal size: $2.1 million ACV, up 28% year-over-year, leveraging our 28 GHz mmWave for ultra-low latency under 5ms. This is huge in Europe, where GDPR-compliant edge computing won us 40% of German auto sector pilots like BMW factories, and in the U.S., logistics firms like UPS are migrating from CBRS to our nationwide coverage.

Overall impact: These launches lifted total revenue growth to 9% year-over-year, with service revenue up 11% to $18.2 billion trailing twelve months. Subscriber trends show postpaid phone net adds of 1.4 million—phone-only ARPU $52—broadband 1.2 million, and converged households up 25% to 8.5 million—our quad-play sweet spot, reducing blended churn to 0.9% from 1.4% a year ago. SAC remains efficient at $350 per sub, 15% below peers, thanks to digital onboarding and eSIM activation. Strategically, we're prioritizing 5G-Advanced readiness with 3GPP Release 18 trials for RedCap IoT and XR media delivery, positioning us against AT&T's fiber pivot and Charter's HFC upgrades. Cross-sell attach rates hit 42%, driving 6% ARPU expansion. Looking forward, we expect Q4 launches—like AI-enhanced 5G Ultra Pack with Apple Vision Pro integration—to add another 3 million subs and $1.5 billion revenue, with EBITDA margins expanding 200 basis points to 42%.

Now, turning to our Content and Media segment performance, which continues to be a cornerstone of our diversified revenue streams. This segment encompasses our direct-to-consumer streaming platforms—NexStream SVOD and NexStream+ premium tier—our FAST channels via NexFree TV, linear cable networks including our flagship sports channel NexSportsNet, and content licensing to third parties like Paramount Global and Warner Bros. Discovery. In Q3, the segment delivered robust performance amid a challenging macroeconomic environment, with streaming subscriber momentum offsetting softer linear TV trends.

Total Content and Media segment revenue reached $2.82 billion, up 12% year-over-year and 4% quarter-over-quarter. This marks our ninth consecutive quarter of double-digit year-over-year growth, driven by a healthy mix of subscription, advertising, and affiliate fee expansion. Subscription revenue—our largest bucket at $1.45 billion, 52% of segment total—grew 18% year-over-year, fueled by net adds and ARPU expansion. NexStream's base pricing adjustments, averaging $1.50 per month across tiers, contributed $120 million incrementally, while bundling with our wireless postpaid plans added another $85 million.

Advertising revenue hit $850 million, 30% of total, up 15% year-over-year. AVOD and FAST monetization shone: NexFree TV, our ad-supported FAST service with 500-plus channels including exclusives like Retro Classics and lifestyle content, generated $210 million, a 45% year-over-year surge thanks to CTV inventory sell-through rates exceeding 92% during prime slots. Political ad spend in the U.S. ahead of midterms boosted this by 8% quarter-over-quarter, mirroring trends at peers like Roku and The Trade Desk. Affiliate and content licensing contributed $530 million, 18% of total, flat year-over-year as linear MVPD declines of $50 million were offset by carriage fee hikes on NexSportsNet—now averaging $4.20 per sub per month, up from $3.90—and syndication deals for our unscripted series to international platforms like BBC iPlayer. Excluding foreign exchange headwinds in EMEA, organic growth was 14% year-over-year. For the nine months year-to-date, segment revenue stands at $8.41 billion, up 13% from prior year.

Adjusted EBITDA for the segment came in at $920 million, delivering a robust 33% margin—up 200 basis points year-over-year from 31%. This expansion reflects operating leverage from scale: content amortization costs as a percentage of revenue fell to 28% from 31%, thanks to better utilization of our $5 billion annual content investment across originals and licensed libraries. Key margin drivers included lower customer acquisition costs at $45 per new streaming sub, down 15% year-over-year via targeted digital marketing and 5G-enabled in-app promotions on our mobile network. Content cost efficiencies from our AI-driven recommendation engine boosted viewer retention by 22%, extending average session times to 45 minutes and reducing churn-related write-offs. Offsetting pressures: Sports rights amortization for NBA and NFL packages rose 10% year-over-year to $320 million in Q3, but we mitigated this with dynamic ad pricing yielding $2.50 CPMs on live events—competitive with ESPN's benchmarks. Free cash flow contribution from the segment was $650 million in Q3, supporting our $15 billion content capex guidance for FY2023.

Our paid digital video subscribers across NexStream SVOD and NexStream+ reached a record 28.7 million, up 1.2 million or 4% quarter-over-quarter and 14% year-over-year—outpacing industry averages from Nielsen data. Domestic U.S. subs grew to 18.2 million, plus 5% quarter-over-quarter, while international hit 10.5 million, plus 2% quarter-over-quarter. Blended digital ARPU expanded to $15.80 per month, up 7% year-over-year, driven by ad-tier upsells at 25% penetration and add-ons like 4K UHD packs at $4.99 a month. Sports bundle ARPU hit $22.50, bolstered by NexSportsNet integration. Monthly churn improved to 3.8%, a 60 basis point year-over-year decline, below the SVOD industry median of 4.5% per Antenna analytics. This reflects our pause feature—allowing 3-month billing suspensions—and personalized content nudges via machine learning. Linear video subs totaled 42 million equivalents, down 3% year-over-year or 1.3 million, in line with cord-cutting trends affecting peers like Charter and DirecTV. However, affiliate revenue per sub held steady at $52 per sub per month. FAST monthly active users exploded to 65 million, up 25% year-over-year, with engagement hours at 8.2 billion—rivaling Tubi's scale and capturing share from traditional broadcast.

North America, 85% of revenue, saw stellar 15% year-over-year growth, led by U.S. streaming adds during NFL season and Hispanic market penetration via Spanish-language FAST channels, up 30% MAUs. Canada saw 10% growth from Rogers partnership bundling. EMEA, 10% of revenue, grew 8% year-over-year to $280 million, despite FX drag. UK and Germany drove 500k net adds via Sky bundling and UEFA Champions League rights. Churn ticked up to 4.2% from regulatory price caps, but we're countering with localized originals like Nordic Noir series. APAC and LATAM, 5% of revenue, showed modest 5% growth to $140 million. Brazil and India FAST launches added 2 million MAUs, but piracy and competition from JioCinema pressured SVOD at plus 1% subs. We're investing $200 million in localization, targeting 20% APAC revenue mix by FY2025.

We're leaning into 5G edge computing for ultra-low latency streaming—our MEC trials reduced buffering by 40% on live sports, boosting concurrency to 15 million peak users. AI personalization, powered by our proprietary StreamGenix engine, lifted content discovery by 35%, directly correlating to a 12% ARPU uplift. Broader trends: FAST/AVOD now 35% of digital revenue, up from 25% year-over-year, capitalizing on ad market recovery with connected TV households projected at 200 million U.S. by 2025 per eMarketer. Linear decline decelerated to minus 3%, versus minus 7% industry, aided by vMVPD wholesale deals with YouTube TV and Hulu + Live TV. Strategically, we're accelerating our Content Everywhere playbook: $1.2 billion in new originals FY2024, like Global Games esports league, plus a JV with the NBA for direct-to-consumer rights starting 2025—aiming to replicate Amazon Prime Video's Thursday Night Football success. M&A pipeline includes bolt-on FAST assets to hit 1,000 channels. Looking forward, we guide Q4 segment revenue growth of 10-12% year-over-year to about $2.9 billion, with EBITDA margins at 34%. Full-year subscriber adds of 4-5 million, targeting 32 million paid digital subs by year-end 2023. Amidst password-sharing crackdowns industry-wide like Netflix's 10 million add-back, we expect further tailwinds. This segment positions NexWave as a streaming pure-play within telco, with ROIC exceeding 20%.

As we dive into the details of our operational performance, I'd like to spend some time on one of our most valuable assets: our spectrum portfolio. Spectrum remains the lifeblood of our wireless business, powering everything from our industry-leading 5G network to our expanding fixed wireless access offerings and media delivery services. We control approximately 1.2 GHz of licensed spectrum across low-, mid-, and high-bands nationwide, including our prized 160 MHz of C-band acquired in the 2021 FCC Auction 107 for $4.6 billion—on par with peers like Verizon and AT&T. This is complemented by 280 MHz of prime mid-band PCS and AWS-3, 600 MHz of low-band sub-1 GHz for coverage, and over 800 MHz of mmWave in our top 30 markets. Our total weighted average spectrum depth is about 140 MHz per POP in covered areas, positioning us competitively against T-Mobile's aggressive mid-band advantage.

On utilization, we're seeing robust demand, with overall network spectrum utilization averaging 78% during peak hours in Q3, up from 72% a year ago. This reflects the explosive growth in 5G data traffic, which surged 45% year-over-year to over 12 exabytes quarterly, driven by video streaming—our NexWave TV+ app alone accounted for 28% of that—and enterprise IoT applications. Mid-band C-band and PCS saw highest utilization at 85%, with median throughput speeds of 450 Mbps down and 60 Mbps up on our 5G SA core. In high-traffic urban cores, we're hitting 92% during evening peaks, comparable to AT&T's reported figures. Low-band steady at 65% utilization, ideal for wide-area coverage but increasingly refarmed for NB-IoT, supporting 2.3 million connected devices for utilities and smart cities. mmWave at 55% utilization in dense deployments, focused on capacity relief for stadiums and arenas, where we've deployed O-RAN compliant small cells with Nokia and Ericsson gear.

Trends are unequivocally positive: 5G adoption now stands at 62% of our postpaid subscribers, up from 48% year-over-year, fueled by our Unlimited 5G+ plans, which bundle NexWave Mobile with ad-supported streaming. Data ARPU rose 8% to $52, while FWA subscribers hit 1.8 million, consuming 150 GB a month on average—mirroring Comcast's Xfinity success but with lower capex intensity at $450 per household passed. Regionally, Northeast and California metros like NYC, LA, and Boston saw 88-95% peak utilization, where C-band is fully deployed across 85% of sites. Here, we're throttling back 4G LTE to free 20 MHz for 5G carrier aggregation, boosting speeds 30%. Southeast and Midwest like Atlanta and Chicago averaged 75%, with strong FWA ramp-up; we've passed 15 million homes, capturing 22% market share versus T-Mobile's 28%. Rural West and Mountain states at 52% utilization, where low-band dominates for coverage. Initiatives like our partnership with EchoStar for Dish Network offload are pushing this toward 70% by year-end.

To maximize these assets, we're executing several technical initiatives. Spectrum refarming repurposed 40 MHz of legacy 2G/3G in sub-1 GHz bands, reallocating it to 5G NR, which improved rural latency by 25% to under 20 ms. Dynamic spectrum sharing with Samsung modems allows seamless 4G/5G multiplexing, extending mid-band capacity by 15-20% without new auctions. We're piloting AI-driven spectrum analytics via AWS Outposts, predicting congestion 30 minutes ahead with 92% accuracy, enabling proactive traffic steering. And in media synergies, we're allocating 100 MHz of CBRS for private 5G networks at venues like Madison Square Garden, streaming 8K content with zero buffering.

Looking ahead to future allocation plans, we're laser-focused on augmentation, optimization, and diversification. We'll bid aggressively in the FCC's upcoming 3.45-3.55 GHz CBRS expansion auction in H1 2025, targeting 60-80 MHz nationally for $2-3 billion to deepen mid-band to 220 MHz per POP. This mirrors T-Mobile's 2.5 GHz windfall and is fully funded via $1.5 billion spectrum backlog amortization. 20% of our low-band will shift to FWA overlay by 2026, supporting 5 million additional homes and generating $800 million incremental revenue at 45% margins. We're also leasing 50 MHz mmWave to enterprise clients like Walmart for private networks, akin to Verizon's model, yielding $150 million annualized. For 6G runway and media innovation, allocating 10-15% of high-band for R&D in O-RAN 7.2 and THz trials with Qualcomm, while reserving C-band slices for edge media compute—think AR/VR streaming for our NexSportsNet. These moves enhance our free cash flow profile: spectrum-driven capex is capped at 14% of revenue in 2025, down from 16%, with ROI on new allocations projected at 25% IRR over five years. Competitors like AT&T are spectrum-constrained post-C-band, giving us a 15% capacity edge in key markets. Risks include regulatory delays on auctions or satellite interference in C-band, but our $2 billion liquidity buffer and hedging mitigate that. Our spectrum assets are highly utilized, strategically optimized, and poised for outsized returns. This underpins our FY25 guidance of 12-15% wireless revenue growth and 18% EBITDA margins.

Thank you. That covers the financial and strategic highlights from my perspective.

Taylor Kim: Thank you, Jordan. I would like to provide an update on our network performance and expansion. We continue to enhance our 5G network, achieving wider coverage and faster speeds. Good morning, everyone, and thanks for joining our Q3 earnings call. Before I dive into the quarter's financials, I'd like to provide a detailed update on our network investments, with a focus on 5G deployment progress and our associated capital expenditures. Our integrated telecom and media strategy hinges on a world-class 5G network that not only powers our wireless subscriber base of 120 million but also enables next-gen media experiences like ultra-low-latency streaming, AR/VR content delivery, and edge computing for our Peacock streaming platform and live sports broadcasts. We've continued to execute aggressively here, balancing aggressive buildout with disciplined spending to drive long-term ARPU uplift and margin expansion.

We're now at 92% nationwide 5G coverage on a population basis in the U.S., up from 85% at the end of Q3 last year—a 7-percentage-point year-over-year increase. This includes sub-6GHz mid-band coverage, which reaches 88% of our footprint and delivers gigabit speeds averaging 450 Mbps downlink in real-world tests, per our latest Ookla Speedtest Intelligence data. For high-density urban areas, our mmWave deployments cover over 15,000 small cells across the top 50 MSAs, providing multi-gigabit speeds exceeding 2 Gbps—critical for enterprise private 5G networks and immersive media applications like 8K live event streaming.

A key milestone this quarter was the acceleration of our 5G Standalone core rollout. We've now deployed SA architecture across 65% of our 5G sites, up from 40% in Q3 2023, leveraging our cloud-native, virtualized RAN stack in partnership with Ericsson and Nokia. This SA progress unlocks network slicing for differentiated services: for consumers, we've sliced for ultra-reliable low-latency communications to support cloud gaming partnerships with Xbox Game Pass, reducing latency to under 20ms; for media, we're slicing for enhanced mobile broadband to prioritize Peacock's 4K/HDR streams during peak events like NFL Sunday Ticket; and for enterprises, private slices are live in 200-plus sites for industries like manufacturing and healthcare.

On the spectrum front, we've optimized our C-band holdings—acquired in the 2021 FCC auction for $9.5 billion—to 85% utilization in deployed markets, achieving spectral efficiency gains of 25% via massive MIMO 64T64R configurations. We're also densifying with Open RAN pilots in the Southeast, where we've integrated Samsung radios with our existing stack, cutting vendor lock-in risks and supporting our goal of 30% Open RAN by 2026. Fiber backhaul is another enabler: we've lit 45,000 route miles of our own dark fiber network this year, ensuring 100Gbps-plus connectivity to 95% of our 5G sites and positioning us for 6G precursors like AI-driven traffic orchestration.

Regionally, Northeast and West Coast metros like NYC, LA, and SF have 100% sub-6GHz and mmWave coverage, with SA at 90%. Here, 5G FWA has onboarded 1.2 million households, stealing share from cable peers with 300Mbps symmetrical speeds at $70 a month—directly competing with Comcast's Xfinity in overlapping markets. Midwest and South like Chicago, Dallas, and Atlanta: sub-6GHz at 95%, mmWave ramping to 40% coverage by year-end. We've deployed 2,500 new sites in these regions, focusing on rural meshing with our 3.45GHz CBRS spectrum for agribusiness IoT. International footprint via our 25% stake in EuroNet Mobile: 5G covers 75% of the UK and Germany combined, with SA trials supporting BBC iPlayer edge caching for sub-5ms latency.

Customer adoption reflects this progress: 72% of our postpaid wireless subs are now on 5G plans, driving a 4.2% year-over-year ARPU increase to $58.50, fueled by Unlimited Ultimate tiers bundling 5G with Peacock Premium. Churn remains best-in-class at 0.76%, and enterprise 5G revenue grew 35% year-over-year to $1.2 billion, including private networks for Disney's AR experiences at theme parks.

For full-year 2024, we're guiding to $17.8 billion in total capex, flat year-over-year but with a higher return profile. Of this, $12.4 billion—or 70%—is allocated to network investments, with $9.2 billion specifically for 5G wireless, up 8% year-over-year. Radio access network at $5.1 billion, up 12%; spectrum and backhaul $2.8 billion, up 5%; core and transport $1.3 billion, flat; fiber and fixed broadband $2.4 billion, up 3%; media and edge infrastructure $0.8 billion, up 15%; maintenance and other $5.4 billion, down 2%. This disciplined approach reflects efficiencies from vRAN, saving 15-20% on opex via software upgrades, and AI/ML for predictive site maintenance, which reduced unplanned outages by 28%. We're below the industry average capex intensity of 18-20% of revenue—ours is 16.5% at $108 billion trailing revenue—thanks to spectrum leverage and FWA scaling, which has a 2-3x ROI versus traditional fiber-to-the-home.

Strategically, these investments are yielding tangible returns. 5G has contributed $2.5 billion in incremental EBITDA over the past 12 months through higher ARPU, lower churn, and new revenue streams like edge computing for media partners—think Verizon-like MEC deals but integrated with our content arm for Peacock's cloud gaming. We're on pace for EBITDA margins to expand 150bps to 48% in 2025, as 5G SA enables 20-30% capacity gains without proportional capex. Looking ahead, 2025 capex guidance will be $18.0-$18.5 billion, with 5G spend shifting to optimization—60% of wireless capex—and 6G R&D like terahertz trials with Qualcomm. We'll continue spectrum advocacy at the FCC for 6GHz unlicensed access, mirroring T-Mobile's mid-band success, and expand private 5G for media production—imagine slicing for live 360-degree NFL streams. Our 5G progress positions NexWave as a leader in converged telecom-media, delivering shareholder value through efficient capex and revenue growth.

Our network reliability remains high, and we are investing in advanced technologies to further improve performance. We are also focused on optimizing our network for emerging applications like IoT and edge computing.
